title: Exploring building materials: human skin as a sensory reference in the absence of visual cues
research_question: This study aimed to explore how people perceive building materials through sense in the absence of visual attention and how texture meanings affect indoor spaciousness perception. It also aimed to investigate the perceptual capabilities of sighted individuals in the absence of visual information and the relationship between wall textures and spatial perception using a multi-sensory approach.

participants.description: Study 1: 38 healthy participants (20 males, 30 females, mean age ±SD: 22 ± 5 years). Study 2: 100 new individuals (64 males, 36 females, mean age ±SD: 22 ± 5 years). Study 3: 10 students.
participants.recruitment: Participants were recruited separately for each study. The experimental protocol received approval from the Ethics Review Committee of the Faculty of Medical Sciences, University of Sri Jayewardenepura. All participants provided written informed consent.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Study 1: Three physical boxes constructed with distinct building materials (Wall putty/smooth, Sand/semi-rough, Aggregate/rough) and a 250-W infrared light bulb administered at three intensity levels (0%, 40%, 100%). Participants placed one hand inside the box.
Study 2: Three physical rooms of the same size (3'x3'x8') with different wall textures (Wall putty/smooth, Sand/semi-rough, Aggregate/rough). Participants navigated blindfolded.
Study 3: Ten real-world locations with diverse wall textures (rough, textured to smooth surfaces). Participants navigated blindfolded.

measures.instrument: Participant self-report of material type after tactile assessment
Self-report rating on a questionnaire (implied Likert-type scale)
Self-report ratings on 8 semantic scales (Temperature, Surface Roughness, Comfort, Preference) using a five-level scoring system
Open-ended participant reflections recorded via voice recorder

implementation_implications: Architects and designers can strategically use texture to enhance the perception of space, creating more inclusive environments that feel more spacious without increasing physical dimensions, potentially reducing material use and construction costs.
Thoughtful material selection in spatial design can optimize occupants' comfort and wellbeing.
Strategic selection of wall finishes can effectively augment the perceived spaciousness of interior environments, supporting more efficient and environmentally conscious architectural practices.
Material design can promote psychological health and comfort through thoughtful material design in architectural spaces.

limitations: Not explicitly stated by the authors in a dedicated section. However, the study design for Study 2 did not use infrared lights or energy ray simulations due to health repercussions, which could be seen as a limitation in terms of controlling all sensory inputs.
crossref_title: Exploring building materials: human skin as a sensory reference in the absence of visual cues
crossref_abstract: Material texture significantly influences how people perceive built environments, yet empirical evidence supporting its impact on spaciousness perception is limited. This study aimed to explore how people perceive building materials through sense in the absence of visual attention and how texture meanings affect indoor spaciousness perception. Conducted with 160 participants (90 males, 70 females, mean age ±SD: 22 ± 5 years), the study comprised three phases: baseline tactile assessment, blindfolded navigation in a lab and exposure to real-world environments. Findings revealed the skin’s ability to discern textural quality without visual cues, with slightly rough wall surfaces consistently perceived as more spacious. Moreover, the association between wall texture and perceived space varied, with subjective aspects influencing spaciousness in relatively spacious rooms, while objective factors played a larger role in less spacious settings. This study provides insights into sensory referral processes, warranting further investigation into the potential psychological impacts of textures.
